title: Google Director Resigns Over Pentagon AI Deal, Says Company Abandoned Its Moral Compass
excerpt: Google director resigns over AI technology deal with the Pentagon, citing ethical concerns.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Google director resigns over AI technology deal with the Pentagon, citing ethical concerns.
  • The Pentagon deal may violate international laws and contradict Google's original AI principles.
  • Growing dissent among Google employees, with hundreds signing letters against military AI work.
  • Indian engineers at Google face unique challenges balancing ethics and job security.
  • Mayrhofer's resignation highlights the ethical dilemmas in AI's military applications.
Ethical Concerns Over Military AI
›Google's AI technology supplied to the Pentagon for classified operations.
›Original AI principles established in 2018 prohibited weapon development.
›Principles revised in February 2025, removing restrictions on military use.
›Mayrhofer warns of potential violations of international laws.
Sources: Livemint, Business Insider
> **"Andreas Kirsch, a Google DeepMind research scientist, told Business Insider in April that he was "incredibly ashamed" of the decision to supply AI for classified military work."**

'I Couldn't Stay in Good Conscience'

A senior Google director has resigned in protest over the company's decision to supply artificial intelligence technology to the US military, warning that the Pentagon deal could ultimately be used against European citizens and that leadership has "quietly abandoned" the ethical principles that once defined the company.

René Mayrhofer, director of Android platform security, confirmed that he circulated a farewell letter to colleagues in May, accusing leadership of reversing commitments on both climate and warfare without internal debate.

The Pentagon Deal That Triggered the Exit

Google announced in late April an agreement with the US Department of Defense to provide AI technology for classified operations, including military planning and intelligence gathering.

"Google management has quietly abandoned the goals to become carbon-neutral because of the AI model energy usage," Mayrhofer wrote. "Worse, the current Google management is now signing deals with the US Ministry of War, where 'any lawful purpose' by the current US government has already been repeatedly demonstrated to be in violation of international laws."

At the center of his grievances is Google's quiet dismantling of its own AI principles. First drawn up in 2018 with pledges not to develop weapons or surveillance tools, those guidelines were revised in February 2025 to remove those restrictions entirely.

Growing Dissent Inside Google

Mayrhofer is not alone. Andreas Kirsch, a Google DeepMind research scientist, told Business Insider in April that he was "incredibly ashamed" of the decision to supply AI for classified military work. Hundreds of employees reportedly signed internal letters objecting.

"I am a pacifist, and have long ago decided that I will not personally work for militaries engaging in offensive warfare," Mayrhofer wrote. "Proactively harming people is not something that I can or will be involved with."

A Google spokesperson said the company was "proud" to support national security and remained committed to ensuring AI would not be used for "domestic mass surveillance or autonomous weaponry without appropriate human oversight."

The Uncomfortable Position for Indian Engineers

The resignation highlights a tension that Indian-origin employees at Google navigate daily. With tens of thousands of Indian engineers at the company — many on H-1B visas that tie immigration status to continued employment — the luxury of principled resignation is one many cannot afford.

Mayrhofer acknowledged this privilege: "As a tenured academic in the EU, I am quite privileged that my decision was only hard because I was balancing the good I could still do vs. tolerating the military angle, but not being dependent on the financial part. Many others are not in that situation."

As AI's role in military and intelligence operations expands, the ethical questions facing the industry's predominantly immigrant workforce will only grow more urgent.
